definition: Say number words in order. Touch one thing for each word you say.
example: Maya has a bowl of grapes. She touches each one and says: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. She counted 5 grapes.
misconception: Kids often skip a number, or touch the same grape twice.

definition: A word or sign that tells how many.
example: Leo draws 3 stars on his paper. Next to them he writes the number 3. The 3 tells how many stars are there.

definition: A bigger amount. One group has extra.
example: Ana has 7 stickers. Sam has 4 stickers. Ana has more, because 7 is a bigger amount than 4.
misconception: Kids may think 'more' means bigger in size. A group of 7 tiny beads is still more than 4 big ones.

visual.alt: An animated bowl overflowing with many colorful balls.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Add & Take Away: How Many More, Slide 5

definition: A smaller amount. One group has less than the other.
example: Ivy picks 3 apples. Ben picks 6 apples. Ivy has fewer apples than Ben.
misconception: 'Fewer' is for things you count one by one. 'Less' is for things you measure, like water.

visual.alt: An animated dog with just one ball.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Add & Take Away: How Many More, Slide 5

definition: The same amount. Not more and not less.
example: Zoe has 3 red blocks. Omar has 3 blue blocks. The groups are equal. Each one has 3.

visual.alt: Three circles each split into 8 equal wedges, showing 2/8, 1/4, and 1/2 shaded.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Fractions, Slide 11 (Visual Vicuna)

definition: A bigger value than another number.
example: Nina rolls an 8. Theo rolls a 5. Nina's number is greater than Theo's, so she moves first.

definition: A smaller value than another number.
example: Sam counts 2 birds on the wire. Maya counts 9. Sam's number is less than Maya's.

definition: The very next number when you count up.
example: Leo has 4 marbles. His mom hands him 1 more. Now he has 5. One more than 4 is 5.

definition: A number that means none at all.
example: The cookie jar had 3 cookies. Ana's family ate every one. Now there are zero cookies left.
misconception: Zero is a real number, not an empty space. It tells you the amount is none.

visual.alt: The numeral 0.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Algebraic Thinking, Slide 34 ("The History of Zero")

definition: Lined up from smallest to biggest.
example: Ana drops her number cards and they get mixed up. She puts them back in order: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

definition: A word that tells the order, like first, second, or third.
example: Leo lines up his toy cars. The red car is first. The blue car is second. The green car is third.

definition: Coming earlier in a line or a count.
example: Ana counts to 10. She knows 4 comes before 5.

definition: Coming later in a line or a count.
example: Ben counts his blocks. He knows 6 comes after 5.

definition: In the middle of two other things.
example: Ivy looks at the number line. She sees that 5 sits between 4 and 6.

definition: The written symbol for a number, like 5 or 12.
example: Leo sees the numeral 7 on the classroom door. It tells him room 7 is his room.
misconception: A numeral is the symbol you write. The number is the amount it stands for.

definition: Not the same amount. One group has more or fewer than the other.
example: Ana has 4 shells and Ben has 6 shells. Their groups are unequal, because 4 and 6 are not the same.

definition: Put groups together. You find how many there are in all.
example: Ben has 2 red cars. He gets 3 blue cars. He adds them together: 2 and 3 make 5 cars.

definition: Take some away. You find how many are left.
example: Ivy has 5 balloons. Two of them pop. She subtracts 2 from 5. Now 3 balloons are left.

definition: The total you get when you add.
example: Zoe finds 2 shells, then 3 more. She adds them. The sum is 5 shells.
misconception: 'Sum' means the answer to adding. Kids sometimes use it for any answer.

definition: Join two groups to make one bigger group.
example: Theo puts together 3 red blocks and 2 blue blocks. Now he has one tower of 5 blocks.

definition: Split one group into smaller groups.
example: Nina has 5 crackers. She takes them apart into a group of 2 and a group of 3.

definition: Break a number into smaller parts. It is a big word for 'break apart'.
example: Omar holds 5 pennies. He decomposes 5 into 4 and 1. He puts 4 in one hand and 1 in the other.
misconception: The word sounds hard, but the job is easy. It just means breaking a number into parts.

definition: A math sentence with an equal sign. It shows two sides that match.
example: Maya writes 3 + 2 = 5. That is an equation. The left side and the right side are worth the same.

definition: Words in a problem that ask for the total.
example: Leo has 4 toy cars. Sam has 2. How many do they have in all? The boys add and find 6.

definition: Words in a problem that ask what is still there.
example: Ana bakes 6 muffins and eats 2. How many are left? She subtracts and finds 4.
misconception: Hunting for key words alone can trick you. Always picture what is really happening in the story.

definition: A set of shapes, colors, or numbers that repeat in the same order.
example: Theo lines up blocks: red, blue, red, blue. He says the pattern will keep going: red, blue, red.
misconception: A pattern needs to repeat more than once. Two shapes in a row are not a pattern yet.

definition: The sign (+) that tells you to add.
example: Maya writes 4 + 3 on her paper. She sees the plus sign and knows to add the two numbers together.

definition: Another word for subtract. It means to take some away.
example: Sam has 5 pretzels and eats 2. He works out 5 minus 2, and finds 3 pretzels left.
misconception: 'Minus' means the same thing as 'take away', even though the two words look nothing alike.

definition: Words that mean to subtract. Some things are removed from a group.
example: Ben has 6 balloons and 2 float away. He works out 6 take away 2, and finds 4 left.

visual.alt: A bar chart comparing Wildwood's 1,393 seats to Mark's Meadow's 682 seats, with the gap between them marked as the difference.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Add & Take Away: How Many More, Slide 3 (Visual Vicuna)

definition: A group of ten ones.
example: Ben lines up 10 straws and wraps a band around them. Now he holds 1 ten.

definition: Single things. You count them one at a time.
example: Ivy builds 13 with straws. She uses 1 bundle of ten, and 3 loose ones.

definition: A number from 11 to 19. Each one is a ten plus some ones.
example: Zoe counts 14 beads. 14 is a teen number. It is 1 ten and 4 ones.

definition: Put parts together to build a number.
example: Theo composes 12. He takes 1 bundle of ten and adds 2 loose ones.

definition: Goes on for more length.
example: Nina lays her pencil beside her eraser. The pencil reaches farther, so the pencil is longer.
misconception: Line up the ends first. If one thing starts ahead, the test is not fair.

definition: Takes up less length.
example: Omar puts his crayon next to a ruler. The crayon stops sooner, so the crayon is shorter.

definition: Goes up higher.
example: Maya stands beside a young tree. The tree rises above her head, so the tree is taller.

definition: Weighs more. It pulls down harder.
example: Leo holds a rock in one hand and a leaf in the other. The rock pulls his hand down. The rock is heavier.
misconception: Big does not always mean heavy. A huge pillow weighs less than a small stone.

definition: Weighs less.
example: Ana holds a feather and a book. The feather is easy to lift, so the feather is lighter.

definition: Find out how big, how long, or how much.
example: Ben measures his desk with blocks. He lays them end to end with no gaps. The desk is 8 blocks long.
misconception: Leave no gaps and no overlaps. Sloppy spacing gives the wrong count.

definition: Look at two things. See how they are the same or different.
example: Ivy compares two ribbons. She lines up the ends. The red one reaches farther, so it is longer.

definition: Put things in groups that go together.
example: Zoe sorts her buttons by color. Red buttons go in one pile. Blue buttons go in another.

definition: A group of things that share something.
example: Theo makes a category for round things. The ball and the coin both go in it.

definition: The form of a thing. It is the outline you see.
example: Nina traces the lid of a jar onto paper. The shape she draws is a circle.

visual.alt: A colorful mosaic of triangles, circles, squares, and other shapes.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Geometry: Figures, Shapes and Angles, Slide 6

definition: A round shape. It has no corners and no straight sides.
example: Omar looks at the clock on the wall. His finger slides all the way around the face with no bumps. It is a circle.

definition: A shape with 3 straight sides and 3 corners.
example: Maya folds her napkin into a triangle. She counts 3 sides and 3 corners.
misconception: A triangle can be tall, wide, or tipped over. It still counts as long as it has 3 straight sides.

visual.alt: A large triangle made of many smaller triangles.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Geometry: Figures, Shapes and Angles, Slide 13

definition: A shape with 4 straight sides. All 4 sides are the same length.
example: Leo checks a sticky note against his ruler. All 4 sides match, so it is a square.

visual.alt: A green square, captioned "It's a green square."
visual.credit: Usable Math — Geometry: Lines and Lines of Symmetry, Slide 7

definition: A shape with 4 straight sides and 4 corners. The sides across from each other match.
example: Ana measures the door. The two tall sides match. The two short sides match too. The door is a rectangle.
misconception: A square is a rectangle too. It is just a special one with all 4 sides the same.

visual.alt: A rectangular soccer field, from a perimeter word problem.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Area and Perimeter, Slide 8

definition: A shape with 6 straight sides.
example: Ben studies a honeycomb up close. Each little cell has 6 sides, so each cell is a hexagon.

definition: A solid shape with 6 square faces.
example: Ivy rolls a number cube. Every face she lands on is a square. She counts 6 faces in all.

definition: A solid shape that is round all over, like a ball.
example: Zoe spins a basketball on her finger. It looks round from every side. It is a sphere.
misconception: A circle is flat. A sphere is solid. A plate is a circle, a marble is a sphere.

definition: Higher up than something else.
example: Theo watches a bird land on a branch. The bird is above the grass.

definition: Lower down than something else.
example: Nina digs in the garden. She finds the roots growing below the soil.

definition: Right next to something.
example: Omar's cat sits beside the dog. The two of them rest side by side on the rug.

definition: The point where two sides meet.
example: Maya runs her finger around a square tile. She feels a sharp point at each corner and counts 4.

definition: A solid, box-like shape with 6 flat, rectangle faces.
example: Theo stacks a tissue box on the shelf. It has 6 flat sides shaped like rectangles. It is a cuboid.
misconception: A cuboid can be tall, short, or a cube. As long as it has 6 rectangle faces, it counts.

definition: A shape you can pick up and hold. It takes up space. Another name for it is a 3D shape.
example: Omar holds a wooden block. He can turn it over in his hands, so it is a solid shape.

definition: A number you add to another number.
example: Leo writes 3 + 4 = 7. The 3 and the 4 are the addends. They are the parts he put together.
misconception: The answer is not an addend. Only the numbers going in are addends.

definition: The answer you get when you add.
example: Ana finds 6 shells, then 2 more. She adds them up. The sum is 8 shells.

definition: The answer you get when you subtract.
example: Gordon Stadium seats 79,407 people. Hillcrest Stadium seats 58,868 people. The difference tells how many more seats Gordon Stadium has: 20,539.
misconception: In math, 'difference' does not mean how two things are unlike. It is the subtraction answer.

visual.alt: A bar chart comparing Wildwood's 1,393 seats to Mark's Meadow's 682 seats, with the gap between them marked as the difference.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Add & Take Away: How Many More, Slide 5 (Hint 4, Visual Vicuna)

definition: A math sentence with an equal sign. Both sides are worth the same.
example: Ivy writes 5 + 3 = 8. Each side of the equal sign is worth 8, so the sentence balances.
misconception: The equal sign does not mean 'here comes the answer'. It means both sides match.

definition: The missing number in a problem. You solve to find it.
example: Zoe sees 4 + ? = 9. The ? is the unknown. She counts up from 4 to 9 and finds 5.

definition: A set of facts built from the same three numbers.
example: Theo uses 3, 4, and 7. His fact family is 3 + 4 = 7, 4 + 3 = 7, 7 - 3 = 4, and 7 - 4 = 3.

definition: Adding a number to itself.
example: Nina has 4 red beads and 4 blue beads. That is a double. She knows 4 + 4 = 8 right away.

definition: Look at two numbers. Tell which is bigger or smaller.
example: Omar compares 6 and 9 on the number line. The 9 sits farther right, so 9 is bigger.

definition: Words that ask about the gap between two amounts.
example: Maya has 8 stickers. Leo has 5. How many more does Maya have? She subtracts and finds 3.

visual.alt: A bar chart comparing Wildwood's 1,393 seats to Mark's Meadow's 682 seats, with the gap between them marked as the difference.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Add & Take Away: How Many More, Slide 3 (Visual Vicuna)

definition: The amount you get when you put everything together.
example: Ivy has 3 red beads and 4 blue beads. She adds them to find the total: 7 beads.

visual.alt: Rows of dog bone treats, from a word problem about a daily total.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Multiplication and Division, Slide 5

definition: Taking one number away from another to find what is left.
example: Zoe uses subtraction to solve 9 - 4. She takes 4 away from 9 and finds 5.
misconception: Subtraction is the name for the operation. 'Subtract' is the action word for doing it.

definition: The value a digit has because of where it sits.
example: Ana writes 47. The 4 sits in the tens place, so it is worth 40. The 7 is worth just 7.
misconception: In 47, the 4 does not mean four. Its spot makes it worth forty.

visual.alt: An animated place-value chart for 52,068: colored counters stack into columns as the digits break out into 5 ten-thousands, 2 thousands, 0 hundreds, 6 tens, and 8 ones.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Place Value, Slide 3

definition: Groups of ten.
example: Ben bundles his straws into groups of ten. He makes 3 bundles. That is 3 tens, or 30.

definition: Single units left over after you make tens.
example: Ivy has 25 beads. She makes 2 bundles of ten and has 5 ones left over.

definition: A sign that points to the bigger number.
example: Zoe writes 8 > 5. The wide open side faces the 8, because 8 is the greater number.

definition: A sign that shows the first number is smaller.
example: Theo writes 3 < 7. The narrow point faces the 3, because 3 is less.
misconception: Think of a hungry mouth. It always opens toward the bigger number.

definition: A sign that shows both sides are worth the same.
example: Nina writes 6 = 6. Both sides match exactly, so the equal sign fits.

definition: Start at one number and keep counting up.
example: Omar has 6 marbles and gets 3 more. He counts on from 6: 7, 8, 9. He has 9.
misconception: Do not start over at 1. Begin at the number you already have.

definition: How long something is from end to end.
example: Maya measures her shoe with paper clips. She lays them end to end. The length is 5 clips.

definition: Find the size of something with a tool or a unit.
example: Leo measures his book with cubes. He lines them up with no gaps and counts 7.

definition: Line things up from shortest to longest.
example: Ana holds three ribbons. She lines up one end of each, then orders them by length.

definition: A unit of time. The short hand on a clock points to it.
example: Ben checks the clock. The short hand is on 3 and the long hand is on 12. It is 3 o'clock.

definition: Thirty minutes. Half of one hour.
example: Ivy looks at the clock. The long hand points straight down at 6. It is half past 2.

definition: Facts you collect and can count.
example: Zoe asks every classmate about their pet. She writes down each answer. Those answers are her data.

definition: A chart that counts with small marks.
example: Theo makes a tally chart of bus riders. He draws one mark per rider. Every fifth mark crosses the other four.

visual.alt: A table pairing the numbers 1 through 10 with their matching tally marks.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Charts and Graphs, Slide 21

definition: A picture that shows data so you can compare.
example: Nina graphs the class pets. The dog bar is the tallest, so dogs are the most common pet.

visual.alt: A dashboard illustration with bar, line, and gauge charts.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Charts and Graphs, Slide 5

definition: How much a container can hold.
example: Leo pours water into a jug until it is full. The amount it holds is its capacity.

definition: A sorting chart with boxes that shows whether something has a property or not.
example: Zoe sorts her buttons in a Carroll diagram: one box for round buttons, one box for buttons that are not round.

definition: Cut a shape into parts.
example: Omar partitions his sandwich. He cuts straight down the middle into 2 equal parts.

definition: Parts that are all the same size.
example: Maya splits a pancake with her sister. Each one gets an equal share. Neither piece is bigger.
misconception: Same number of pieces is not enough. The pieces have to be the same size too.

definition: Two equal parts of one whole.
example: Leo cuts an apple into halves. Each piece is one of two equal parts.

definition: One of two equal parts of a whole.
example: Sam cuts his sandwich into 2 equal parts and eats half.
misconception: A piece only counts as 'half' if both pieces are the same size. Two uneven pieces are not halves.

definition: Four equal parts of one whole.
example: Ana cuts a pizza into fourths. She and 3 friends each take one part.

definition: Another word for fourths.
example: Ben folds his paper in half, then in half again. He opens it up and finds 4 quarters.

definition: Something you can notice about a shape, like its sides or corners.
example: Ivy looks at a triangle. She names two attributes: 3 sides and 3 corners.

definition: A flat shape. It has length and width but no thickness.
example: Zoe draws a square on paper. It lies flat on the page, so it is a 2D shape.

definition: A solid shape you can hold. It takes up space.
example: Theo picks up a wooden cube. He can turn it over in his hand, so it is a 3D shape.

definition: The point where two sides of a shape meet. The plural is vertices.
example: Zoe traces a triangle with her finger. She counts 3 corners, or vertices, where the sides meet.

visual.alt: A cube's 8 corners marked as colored dots.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Geometry: Figures, Shapes and Angles, Slide 3 (Visual Vicuna)

definition: A turn of one-fourth of the way around, like turning to face a new wall.
example: Omar faces the window. He makes a quarter turn and now faces the door.

definition: A turn of halfway around, so you end up facing the opposite way.
example: Maya faces the front of the room. She makes a half turn and now faces the back wall.

definition: Adding the same number again and again.
example: Nina sets out 4 plates and puts 3 grapes on each. She adds 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 and gets 12 grapes.

definition: Putting numbers together to find a total. You can add two numbers, or add the same number many times.
example: A science class collects rocks and puts them into 5 buckets, 70 rocks in each one. Chef Math Bear adds the numbers to find the total: 70 + 70 + 70 + 70 + 70 = 350 rocks.
misconception: Adding the same number again and again is still addition. It only becomes multiplication once you count how many equal groups you have, instead of adding them one at a time.

visual.alt: A chalkboard showing 70 written five times, stacked above a plus sign and a question mark, captioned "Add the numbers."
visual.credit: Usable Math — Multiplication and Division, Slide 2 (Hint 2, Chef Math Bear)

definition: Objects set out in equal rows and columns.
example: Omar lines up his stickers in 3 rows of 5. That is an array. He counts 15 stickers.
misconception: Every row must hold the same amount. A ragged grid is not an array.

definition: A number that splits into two equal groups with none left over.
example: Maya pairs up her 8 socks. She makes 4 pairs with nothing left over, so 8 is even.

definition: A number that leaves one extra when you split it in two.
example: Leo tries to pair up 7 crackers. He makes 3 pairs and 1 is left alone, so 7 is odd.

definition: A problem you solve in two moves.
example: Ana has 10 pencils. She buys 5 more, then gives 3 to Ben. First she adds to get 15. Then she subtracts to get 12.
misconception: Stopping after the first step is the usual slip. Reread the question to check you finished.

definition: The number you are missing. A letter or a box can stand in for it.
example: Ivy sees 12 - ? = 7. She asks herself what takes 12 down to 7. The unknown number is 5.

definition: A pair of numbers that add up to a target number.
example: Omar learns the number bonds for 10: 6 and 4, 7 and 3, 8 and 2. Each pair adds up to 10.

definition: Groups of one hundred.
example: Zoe counts 342 pennies. She stacks them and finds 3 hundreds, 4 tens, and 2 ones.

definition: A number written as the sum of what each digit is worth.
example: Theo writes 254 in expanded form: 200 + 50 + 4.

definition: What a digit is worth based on its spot.
example: Nina looks at 528. The 5 sits in the hundreds place, so it is worth 500.

definition: Trade ten of one unit for one of the next unit.
example: Omar adds 27 + 15. The ones make 12. He regroups 10 of them into 1 ten and writes 42.

definition: Decide which number is bigger by checking place value.
example: Maya compares 431 and 419. The hundreds match, so she checks the tens. 3 beats 1, so 431 is bigger.
misconception: More digits usually means bigger, but only when you start from the biggest place. Compare left to right.

definition: A grid that shows the numbers 1 to 100 in order.
example: Leo uses a hundred chart to skip count by 10s. He taps 10, 20, 30, all the way down one column.

definition: The biggest number you can make or find in a group.
example: Ana has the digits 3, 7, and 1. She arranges them to make 731, the greatest number she can build.

definition: The tiniest number you can make or find in a group.
example: Ben has the digits 3, 7, and 1. He arranges them to make 137, the smallest number he can build.

definition: Arrange numbers from smallest to biggest, or biggest to smallest.
example: Ana lines up the numbers 52, 18, and 40 in order: 18, 40, 52.

definition: A small unit of length. It is about as wide as your fingernail.
example: Leo lays his crayon along a ruler. The crayon is 9 centimeters long.

visual.alt: A tape measure next to small tools.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Measurement, Slide 8

definition: A larger unit of length. It is about as wide as a door.
example: Ana measures the rug with a meter stick. She steps it out twice, so the rug is 2 meters long.

visual.alt: Runners racing on a track, a distance measured in meters.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Measurement, Slide 8

definition: A smart guess that is close, not exact.
example: Ben looks at a jar of beans and guesses about 50. The real count is 46, so his estimate was close.
misconception: An estimate is not a wild guess. Use what you know to get near the real amount.

definition: A line with numbers spaced out in order.
example: Ivy starts at 8 on the number line and hops to 13. She counts 5 hops.

visual.alt: A number line from 0 to 1 with four labeled points.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Algebraic Thinking, Slide 39

definition: A graph that uses bars to show amounts.
example: Zoe makes a bar graph of favorite fruits. The apple bar rises highest, so apples won.

visual.alt: A bar graph with four colored bars of different heights.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Charts and Graphs, Slide 3

definition: A graph that uses pictures to stand for amounts.
example: Theo draws a picture graph of books read. Each little book stands for 1 real book.

definition: A graph that stacks marks above a number line.
example: Nina measures 10 leaves and marks an X above each length. Most of the X's stack above 4 centimeters.

definition: A unit of money worth 100 cents.
example: Omar saves 4 quarters in a jar. Together they make 1 dollar.

visual.alt: Three comic books priced at $1.00, $2.00, and $2.25.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Money, Slide 18

definition: A coin worth 25 cents.
example: Maya has 3 quarters. She counts 25, 50, 75. She has 75 cents.

definition: A small unit of money. 100 cents make 1 dollar.
example: Omar counts 3 dimes. Each dime is 10 cents, so he has 30 cents.

visual.alt: Three comic books priced at $1.00, $2.00, and $2.25.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Money, Slide 18

definition: Coins and bills used to buy and sell things.
example: Maya counts her money before the school fair: 2 dollar bills and 3 quarters.

visual.alt: An illustration of stacked cash and coins.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Money, Slide 5

definition: How much money something costs.
example: Leo checks the price tag on a toy car. It costs 4 dollars.

visual.alt: Toy figures on a store shelf, from the toy-store price problem.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Money, Slide 16

definition: Two circles that overlap, used to sort things and show what they share.
example: Leo draws a Venn diagram. One circle is red things, one circle is round things. The apple goes where the circles overlap.

definition: India's unit of money.
example: Ana saves 50 rupees from her allowance.

definition: A small unit of Indian money. 100 paise make 1 rupee.
example: Ben has 1 rupee, which is the same as 100 paise.

definition: The value printed on a coin or bill.
example: Ivy sorts her play money by denomination: all the $1 bills together, all the $5 bills together.

definition: A closed shape with 4 straight sides.
example: Leo sorts his shape cards. The square, the rectangle, and the kite all go in one pile. Each has 4 sides.

definition: A closed shape with 5 straight sides.
example: Ana traces home plate at the ball field. She counts 5 sides, so it is a pentagon.

definition: Rows go across. Columns go up and down.
example: Ben sets up chairs in 4 rows and 6 columns. He counts 24 chairs in all.

definition: Parts of one whole that are all the same size.
example: Ivy cuts a brownie into 4 equal shares. Each friend gets a piece the same size.

definition: Add equal groups the fast way.
example: Zoe packs 6 boxes with 4 markers in each. Instead of adding six times, she multiplies 6 × 4 and gets 24.

definition: A number you multiply.
example: Theo writes 3 × 8 = 24. The 3 and the 8 are the factors.

definition: The answer when you multiply.
example: Nina multiplies 5 × 7. The product is 35.

definition: Split into equal groups.
example: Omar has 12 grapes and 3 friends. He divides them evenly, so each friend gets 4.

visual.alt: An animation dividing 52 cupcakes into 8 boxes, with some left over.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Multiplication and Division, Slide 19 (Visual Vicuna)

definition: The answer when you divide.
example: Maya divides 20 by 4. The quotient is 5.

definition: Splitting a number into equal groups. It is the opposite of multiplying.
example: Nina uses division to share 18 cookies among 3 friends. Each friend gets 6.
misconception: Division is the name for the operation. 'Divide' is the action word for doing it.

visual.alt: An animation dividing 52 cupcakes into 8 boxes, with some left over.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Multiplication and Division, Slide 19 (Visual Vicuna)

definition: Putting equal groups together to find a total. It is the opposite of dividing.
example: Corn muffins cost 2 dollars each. Blueberry muffins cost 3 dollars each. Chef Math Bear multiplies to find each cost: 8 x 2 = 16, and 7 x 3 = 21.
misconception: Multiplication is not just fast addition. It counts equal groups all at once, instead of one at a time.

visual.alt: Chef Math Bear's strategy: multiply to find the cost of 8 corn muffins at $2 each, multiply to find the cost of 7 blueberry muffins at $3 each, then add the two costs.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Algebraic Thinking, Slide 16 (Hint 2, Chef Math Bear)

definition: Groups that all hold the same amount.
example: Leo sorts 15 crayons into 3 equal groups. Each group holds 5 crayons.

definition: Objects in equal rows and columns. It shows a multiplication fact.
example: Ana draws 4 rows of 6 dots. Her array shows 4 × 6 = 24.

definition: A rectangle drawing that shows a multiplication problem.
example: Ben draws a rectangle 3 units tall and 5 units wide. He counts 15 squares inside. His area model shows 3 × 5 = 15.

definition: The missing number in a multiplication fact.
example: Ivy sees 4 × ? = 28. She counts by fours until she reaches 28. The unknown factor is 7.

definition: A chart of multiplication facts, also called a times table.
example: Theo studies the multiplication table for 5s to learn 5 x 1 up to 5 x 12 by heart.

definition: A list that shows the price of items, used to find the total cost.
example: Ana uses a rate chart to see that pencils cost 5 rupees each, then finds that 3 pencils cost 15 rupees.

definition: An action that undoes another action. Adding and taking away undo each other.
example: Omar adds 6 + 3 to get 9. He checks it with the inverse: 9 - 3 gets him back to 6.

definition: Make sure an answer is right, often by working it a different way.
example: Maya solves 15 - 7 = 8. To check, she adds 8 + 7 and gets back to 15.
misconception: Checking is not redoing the exact same steps. Using the inverse operation catches more mistakes.

definition: A set amount added each time you count up.
example: Leo counts by 5s: 5, 10, 15, 20. Each increment adds 5 more.

definition: Change a number to a nearby easier one.
example: Zoe rounds 47 to the nearest ten. On the number line 47 sits closer to 50 than to 40, so she rounds up.
misconception: Look at where the number really sits. Do not just chop the last digit off.

definition: Changing a number to a nearby ten or hundred, to make it easier to work with.
example: Ben is rounding 63. On the number line, 63 sits closer to 60 than to 70, so he rounds down to 60.

visual.alt: Rows of colored pencils, from a rounding word problem about packs of pencils.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Estimation, Slide 5

definition: What a digit is worth because of its spot.
example: Theo looks at 528. The 2 sits in the tens place, so it is worth 20.

definition: A number that names part of a whole.
example: Nina cuts a pie into 4 equal slices and takes 1. She ate 1/4 of the pie.
misconception: The parts have to be equal. Four uneven slices do not make fourths.

visual.alt: A chocolate cake marked with lines dividing it into 8 equal slices.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Fractions, Slide 5

definition: The top number. It counts the parts you have.
example: Omar eats 3 slices out of 8. He writes 3/8. The numerator 3 is how many he ate.

definition: The bottom number. It tells how many equal parts make the whole.
example: Maya writes 3/8. The denominator 8 means the whole pie was cut into 8 equal parts.

definition: A fraction with 1 on top. It is one single part.
example: Leo cuts a ribbon into 5 equal pieces and picks up one. He holds 1/5, a unit fraction.

definition: Different fractions that name the same amount.
example: Ana eats 1/2 of a pizza. Ben eats 2/4 of a pizza the same size. They both ate the same amount.

definition: All of the parts together. One complete thing.
example: Ivy has 4 quarter slices of an orange. Put back together they make one whole orange.

definition: Split something into equal parts.
example: Zoe partitions a paper strip into 6 equal parts. Now each part is 1/6 of the strip.

definition: Decide which fraction is larger.
example: Theo compares 1/3 and 1/5 of the same cake. Fewer slices means bigger slices, so 1/3 is more.
misconception: A bigger bottom number does not mean a bigger piece. It means the whole was cut into more, smaller parts.

definition: The amount of flat space a shape covers.
example: Nina tiles a table top with square tiles. She counts 24 tiles, so the area is 24 square units.
misconception: Area is the space inside. Perimeter is the trip around the edge.

visual.alt: A 10-by-10 grid of squares, for counting area.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Area and Perimeter, Slide 6

definition: The distance all the way around a shape.
example: Omar walks around a square garden. Each side takes 5 steps, so the perimeter is 20 steps.

definition: One square used to measure area.
example: Maya covers a card with squares, leaving no gaps. Each one is a square unit. She counts 12.

definition: How much time has passed.
example: Leo starts reading at 2:00 and stops at 2:45. The elapsed time is 45 minutes.

definition: How much liquid a container holds.
example: Ana fills a bottle from the jug. The bottle holds 1 liter, so that is its liquid volume.

definition: How much matter is in an object.
example: Ben sets an apple on the scale. Its mass is 150 grams.

definition: A graph where one picture or step stands for more than one thing.
example: Ivy makes a graph where each square stands for 5 books. A bar 4 squares tall means 20 books.
misconception: Count the value of each step, not the number of steps.

definition: A metric unit of mass equal to 1,000 grams.
example: Zoe weighs a bag of rice. It has a mass of 2 kilograms.

visual.alt: A bathroom scale, for measuring weight in kilograms.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Measurement, Slide 8

definition: A customary unit of length. It is about as long as one big step.
example: Ivy measures the hallway with a yardstick. It is 12 yards long.

visual.alt: A close-up of a tape measure's markings.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Measurement, Slide 12

definition: A fixed unit of measurement that everyone agrees on, like a centimeter.
example: Nina measures her desk in centimeters, a standard unit, so her measurement means the same thing to everyone.

definition: An everyday object used to measure, like a hand span or a paperclip, before using standard units.
example: Omar measures his desk using hand spans, a non-standard unit, before he learns to use a ruler.
misconception: A hand span is different for every person, so measurements made with it will not match.

definition: A closed shape with exactly 4 straight sides.
example: Zoe drops shapes into a hoop labeled 4 sides. Squares, rectangles, and rhombuses all belong.

definition: A group whose members share a trait.
example: Theo makes a category for shapes with 4 sides. The square and the rectangle both belong in it.

definition: A feature of a shape you can name.
example: Nina looks at a rectangle. She names two attributes. It has 4 square corners, and the sides across from each other match.

definition: A closed flat shape made only of straight sides.
example: Maya sorts shapes into a group of polygons: triangles, squares, and hexagons, because they all have straight sides.
misconception: A circle is not a polygon because its side is curved, not straight.

definition: A line that connects two corners of a shape that are not already next to each other.
example: Leo draws a diagonal across a rectangle. It joins two corners that are not next to each other.

definition: Covering a flat surface with shapes that fit together with no gaps or overlaps.
example: Ana notices the tiles on the floor form a tessellation. The squares fit together perfectly with no gaps.

definition: A number that divides into another with nothing left over.
example: Omar tests 12. He finds 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12 all divide it evenly. Those are the factors of 12.

definition: What you get when you multiply a number by a whole number.
example: Maya skip counts by 4: 4, 8, 12, 16. Each number she lands on is a multiple of 4.
misconception: Factors are smaller and divide in. Multiples are bigger and count up.

definition: A number with exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
example: Leo tries to split 7 counters into equal groups. Only 1 group of 7 works. So 7 is prime.
misconception: The number 1 is not prime. It has only one factor, not two.

visual.alt: The number 7 painted in yellow on pavement — a prime number.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Algebraic Thinking, Slide 32 (Hint 2)

definition: A number with more than two factors.
example: Ana splits 12 counters into 2 groups of 6, then into 3 groups of 4. Many splits work, so 12 is composite.

definition: A problem that needs more than one step.
example: Ben buys 3 packs of 8 pencils, then gives 5 away. First he multiplies to get 24. Then he subtracts to get 19.

definition: The amount left over after dividing.
example: Ivy shares 17 stickers with 5 friends. Each one gets 3, and the remainder is 2.

definition: What is still there after dividing into equal groups, with not enough for one more full group.
example: Leo splits 14 pencils into groups of 4. He makes 3 full groups, with 2 pencils left over.
misconception: 'Left over' and 'remainder' mean the same thing. Remainder is just the math word for it.

visual.alt: An animation dividing 47 strawberries into 5 baskets, with 2 left over.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Multiplication and Division, Slide 11 (Visual Vicuna)

definition: A letter that stands for a number you do not know yet.
example: Zoe writes 6 × n = 42. The letter n is the variable. She solves it and finds n = 7.

definition: A math sentence with an equal sign, built from a word problem. A letter can stand for the number you are solving for.
example: Corn muffins cost $2 each and blueberry muffins cost $3 each. To find the total cost m of 8 corn muffins and 7 blueberry muffins, Chef Math Bear writes the equation (2 x 8) + (3 x 7) = m.
misconception: The letter in an equation is not always x. Here it is m, standing in for the total cost - any letter can hold a missing number's place.

visual.alt: Chef Math Bear's strategy: multiply to find the cost of 8 corn muffins at $2 each, multiply to find the cost of 7 blueberry muffins at $3 each, then add the two costs.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Algebraic Thinking, Slide 16 (Hint 2, Chef Math Bear)

definition: Two numbers that multiply together to make a given number.
example: Ben finds the factor pairs of 12: 1 and 12, 2 and 6, 3 and 4.

definition: What each digit is worth based on its position.
example: Theo studies 5,283. The 5 sits in the thousands place, so it is worth 5,000.

definition: A number with more than one digit.
example: Nina adds 3,472 and 1,915. Both are multi-digit numbers, so she lines up the places before she starts.

definition: The usual step by step way to work a problem on paper.
example: Omar multiplies 34 × 26. He uses the standard algorithm, working one place at a time and carrying when needed.

definition: A set of steps that always gets you to the answer, done in the same order every time.
example: Nina follows an algorithm every time she adds two big numbers. First she lines up the places. Then she adds one column at a time.
misconception: An algorithm is not one fixed set of steps for every problem. Different kinds of problems can each have their own algorithm.

definition: The number symbols 0 through 9 that we use every day, written in a base-ten system.
example: Theo writes 2,048 using Hindu-Arabic numbers. Each digit's place tells how much it is worth.

visual.alt: A child surrounded by the playful digits 0 through 9.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Algebraic Thinking, Slide 33

definition: A fraction that names the same amount as another.
example: Maya has 2/4 of a chocolate bar. Leo has 1/2 of the same bar. Their pieces are exactly the same size.

definition: A whole number joined with a fraction.
example: Ana pours 2 full glasses of juice and half of a third. She has 2 1/2 glasses.

definition: A fraction whose top number is bigger than its bottom.
example: Ben has 5 quarter slices of pie. He writes 5/4, which is more than one whole pie.
misconception: An improper fraction is not wrong. It is just written as parts instead of wholes.

definition: A fraction with a top number smaller than its bottom number. It is less than one whole.
example: Zoe writes 3/4 for the pizza slices she ate. Since 3 is smaller than 4, it is a proper fraction.
misconception: A proper fraction is not 'more correct' than an improper one. It just names an amount less than a whole.

visual.alt: An animated tally of 7 boxes filling in with tulip icons, one at a time.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Fractions, Slide 17 (Visual Vicuna)

definition: A shared bottom number for two fractions.
example: Ivy adds 1/3 and 1/4. She rewrites them as 4/12 and 3/12. Now they share a denominator, so she can add.

definition: A number that uses a dot to show parts smaller than one.
example: Zoe reads a price tag: $2.75. The dot separates the whole dollars from the cents.

definition: One whole split into 10 equal parts.
example: Theo shades 3 strips out of 10. He shaded 3 tenths, which he writes as 0.3.

definition: One whole split into 100 equal parts.
example: Nina shades 25 little squares on a grid of 100. She shaded 25 hundredths, or 0.25.

definition: A well known fraction you use to judge others.
example: Omar wonders how big 5/8 is. He compares it to 1/2, a benchmark. 5/8 is a little more than half.

definition: The corner shape made where two rays meet.
example: Maya opens a pair of scissors. The space between the blades forms an angle.
misconception: Longer arms do not make a bigger angle. Only the spread between them counts.

definition: The unit used to measure an angle.
example: Leo measures a square corner with his protractor. It reads 90 degrees.

definition: A tool for measuring angles.
example: Ana lines up the middle of her protractor with the corner. She reads 45 degrees.

definition: The total distance around the outside of a shape.
example: Ben fences a garden 8 feet by 3 feet. He adds 8 + 3 + 8 + 3 and needs 22 feet of fence.

visual.alt: An aerial view of a stadium track and field, its running track forming the perimeter.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Area and Perimeter, Slide 8

definition: A rule written with symbols that works every time.
example: Ivy uses the formula for area: length × width. Her rug is 6 by 4, so the area is 24.

definition: Changing a measure into a different unit.
example: Zoe has 3 feet of ribbon and needs inches. She multiplies 3 × 12 and gets 36 inches.

definition: The two 12-hour halves of the day. A.M. is before noon. P.M. is after noon.
example: Maya wakes up at 7 A.M. and goes to bed at 8 P.M.
misconception: Noon is 12 P.M. and midnight is 12 A.M., which trips kids up since there is no 12 in between.

definition: A way of telling time using the numbers 00:00 to 23:59, with no A.M. or P.M.
example: Leo reads a train schedule that uses the 24-hour clock. 14:00 means 2 P.M.

definition: A metric unit for long distances. It equals 1,000 meters.
example: Maya's family drives 5 kilometers to the lake, much farther than she could walk.

definition: An exact spot. It has no size at all.
example: Theo marks a dot on the map where the library sits. That dot is a point.

definition: A straight path that goes on forever both ways.
example: Nina draws a straight path and puts an arrow on each end. The arrows show the line never stops.

definition: A straight path with one end. It goes on forever the other way.
example: Omar shines a flashlight. The beam starts at the bulb and keeps going, much like a ray.

definition: An angle smaller than a square corner.
example: Maya opens a book just a crack. The narrow angle at the spine is acute.

visual.alt: An acute angle drawn next to a right angle for comparison.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Geometry: Figures, Shapes and Angles, Slide 11

definition: An angle bigger than a square corner.
example: Leo leans a chair back until it nearly lies flat. The wide angle it makes is obtuse.

definition: A square corner. It measures 90 degrees.
example: Ana checks the corner of her paper against a tile. They match exactly, so it is a right angle.

definition: A triangle with all 3 sides the same length.
example: Ben checks a triangle tile with his ruler. All 3 sides measure 4 centimeters, so it is equilateral.

definition: A triangle with exactly 2 sides the same length.
example: Ivy measures a triangle flag. Two sides are 6 inches, and the third is 4 inches, so it is isosceles.
misconception: A triangle can be isosceles even if it does not look symmetrical at first glance. Check the side lengths, not just the shape.

visual.alt: A tall ice cream cone, its two slanted sides the same length.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Geometry: Figures, Shapes and Angles, Slide 13

definition: Lines that stay the same distance apart and never meet.
example: Ben looks down the train tracks. The rails run side by side forever, so they are parallel.

visual.alt: Two striped beach chairs, their stripes running parallel.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Geometry: Lines and Lines of Symmetry, Slide 5

definition: Lines that cross and make a square corner.
example: Ivy studies the window frame. The upright meets the sill at a square corner, so those lines are perpendicular.

visual.alt: Two lines crossing at a right angle.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Geometry: Lines and Lines of Symmetry, Slide 3

definition: A line that folds a shape into two matching halves.
example: Zoe folds a paper heart down the middle. The two halves match exactly, so the fold is a line of symmetry.
misconception: Not every fold works. The halves have to land on each other exactly.

definition: The distance from the center of a circle to its edge.
example: Theo measures from the center of a pizza to its crust. That distance is the radius.

definition: The distance across a circle, through its center. It is twice the radius.
example: Nina measures straight across a round table, through the middle. That distance is the diameter.
misconception: The diameter has to pass through the center. Any line across the circle that misses the center is shorter.

definition: The distance around a circle.
example: Omar wraps a string around a can to measure the circumference.

definition: A flat pattern that can be folded up to make a solid shape.
example: Maya cuts out a net of six squares and folds it up into a cube.

definition: When one half of a shape is the mirror image of the other half.
example: Leo folds a paper butterfly down the middle. Both wings match exactly, so it has reflection symmetry.

definition: Drawings that show what a solid object looks like from different directions.
example: Ana draws her toy box from the top, from the front, and from the side to show all three views.

definition: The agreed order for working a problem. Do parentheses first. Then multiply and divide. Add and subtract last.
example: Theo solves 2 + 3 × 4. He multiplies first and gets 12. Then he adds 2 for a total of 14.
misconception: Working left to right gives 20 here, which is wrong. Multiplying comes before adding.

definition: Curved marks that show what to work out first.
example: Nina solves (2 + 3) × 4. The parentheses come first, so she gets 5. Then 5 × 4 gives 20.

definition: A math phrase with numbers and signs. It has no equal sign.
example: Omar writes 6 × (2 + 1). That is an expression, not an equation.

definition: Work out what an expression is worth.
example: Maya evaluates 4 × (3 + 2). Inside the parentheses gives 5. Then 4 × 5 gives 20.

definition: A list of numbers that follows a rule.
example: Leo starts at 3 and adds 5 each time: 3, 8, 13, 18. His pattern grows by 5.

definition: Two numbers that locate a point on a grid.
example: Ana plots (4, 3). She moves 4 across, then 3 up, and marks the spot.

definition: A number made by multiplying a whole number by itself.
example: Zoe multiplies 6 x 6 and gets 36. 36 is a square number.

definition: A number made by multiplying a whole number by itself three times.
example: Theo multiplies 3 x 3 x 3 and gets 27. 27 is a cube number.

definition: A number that can be arranged as dots in a triangle, like 1, 3, 6, 10.
example: Nina stacks dots in rows of 1, then 2, then 3. The running totals, 1, 3, 6, are triangular numbers.

definition: A small raised number. It tells how many times to multiply the base by itself.
example: Ben writes 10 with a small 3 above it. The exponent means 10 × 10 × 10, which is 1,000.
misconception: An exponent is not the same as multiplying by 3. It means three tens multiplied together.

definition: What you get when you multiply 10 by itself.
example: Ivy sees that 100 is 10 × 10. That makes 100 a power of ten.

definition: Change a decimal to a nearby simpler one.
example: Zoe rounds 3.67 to the nearest tenth. The 7 pushes it up, so she writes 3.7.

definition: Multiply as you would whole numbers. Then place the dot.
example: Theo multiplies 0.4 × 0.3. He thinks 4 × 3 = 12. Two decimal places give him 0.12.
misconception: The answer can be smaller than what you started with. Multiplying by a part shrinks it.

definition: Split a decimal into equal parts.
example: Nina pours 4.5 liters into 3 bottles evenly. Each bottle gets 1.5 liters.

definition: A place value equal to one-thousandth of a whole. It is the third digit after the decimal point.
example: Omar writes 0.125. The 5 is in the thousandths place.

definition: An Indian place-value unit equal to 100,000.
example: Maya reads that a car costs 5 lakh rupees, which means 500,000 rupees.

definition: An Indian place-value unit equal to 10,000,000.
example: Leo reads that a stadium cost 50 crore rupees to build, which means 500,000,000 rupees.

definition: A shared bottom number that lets you add or compare fractions.
example: Omar adds 1/2 and 1/3. He rewrites them as 3/6 and 2/6, then adds to get 5/6.
misconception: You cannot add the bottom numbers. Make them match first, then add only the tops.

definition: A whole number plus a fraction.
example: Maya runs 3 whole laps and half of another. She ran 3 1/2 laps.

definition: Multiply the top numbers. Then multiply the bottom numbers.
example: Leo scoops 1/2 of a 1/3 cup measure. He multiplies and finds he has 1/6 of a cup.

definition: Split a fraction into equal parts, or find how many fit inside.
example: Ana has 1/2 a pizza and shares it with 2 people. Each one gets 1/4 of the pizza.

definition: Write a fraction with the smallest numbers that still name the same amount.
example: Ben has 6/8 of a bar. He divides the top and bottom by 2 and writes 3/4.

definition: The fraction you get when you flip one over.
example: Ivy flips 2/5 and gets 5/2. That is the reciprocal. The two of them multiply to 1.

definition: A fraction expressed as parts per hundred, written with a % sign.
example: Ana scores 90% on her spelling test. Out of 100 equal parts, she got 90 of them right.

definition: The amount of space a solid takes up.
example: Zoe fills a box with unit cubes. It holds 3 layers of 8, so the volume is 24 cubic units.
misconception: Volume fills the inside. Area only covers a flat surface.

definition: One cube used to measure volume.
example: Theo stacks cubes inside a box with no gaps. Each cube is one cubic unit, and he counts 18.

definition: Change a measure to a different unit.
example: Nina has 2,000 meters left to run. She converts it and sees that is just 2 kilometers.

definition: A unit used to measure the speed of a boat or the wind. It is not a unit of length.
example: Omar reads that a ship is sailing at 12 knots, meaning it covers 12 nautical miles every hour.
misconception: A knot already means a speed, not a distance. Nobody says 'knots per hour'.

definition: A grid made by two number lines that cross.
example: Omar maps his neighborhood on a coordinate plane. He finds the park at (4, 3).

definition: The number line that runs across the grid.
example: Maya moves right along the x-axis to 5 before she moves up at all.

definition: The number line that runs up and down the grid.
example: Leo counts up the y-axis to 4 to finish plotting his point.

definition: A grid for locating points. A level line and an upright line cross to make it.
example: Ana plots (4, 3) on the coordinate plane. She goes 4 across, then 3 up.

definition: Two numbers in order that give a point's spot. The across number comes first.
example: Ben plots (2, 5). He moves 2 across, then 5 up. The order changes where he lands.
misconception: Swapping the numbers lands you somewhere else. (2, 5) is not the same as (5, 2).

visual.alt: A blank coordinate grid with labeled x and y axes.
visual.credit: Usable Math — Geometry: Maps + Grids + Ordered Pairs, Slide 11 (Visual Vicuna)

definition: Sort shapes into groups by what they have in common.
example: Ivy classifies triangles by their angles. She makes one pile each for acute, right, and obtuse.

definition: A way to order shape groups. Smaller groups fit inside bigger ones.
example: Zoe draws a chart of shapes. Squares fit inside rectangles, and rectangles fit inside quadrilaterals.
misconception: Every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square.

definition: One of the four sections made when a coordinate plane is divided by its axes.
example: Theo plots a point with two positive coordinates. It lands in the first quadrant.

definition: When a shape looks the same after being turned part of the way around its center.
example: Omar spins a pinwheel shape a third of the way around. It looks exactly the same, so it has rotation symmetry.

definition: A polygon where all the sides and all the angles are equal.
example: Maya checks a hexagon tile. All the sides and all the angles match, so it is a regular polygon.

definition: A polygon where the sides and angles are not all equal.
example: Leo draws a five-sided shape. Its sides are not all the same length, so it is an irregular polygon.

definition: An angle greater than 180 degrees but less than 360 degrees.
example: A door swings almost all the way open. Ana measures the angle: 300 degrees. That is a reflex angle.
misconception: Kids often measure the small angle instead of the wide one. A reflex angle is always the bigger way around.
